No quantity-insensitive determinate rule exists. Source picture (Lindskoog & Brend 1962:39): stress the first syllable always; stress every heavy syllable (CVC, CVV(C), but not CVʔ); optionally stress any remaining nonfinal syllable; plus obligatory stress on stem-initial syllables and lexically stressed suffixes. Not codable as one stress string per word length.

59.heavy: heavy syllable = CVC or CVV(C); a syllable closed only by glottal stop (CVʔ) is NOT heavy. (p. 38 adds: within-syllable Vi clusters carry stress on the first vowel only.)

59.srule: Further stresses (not ranked as 'secondary' by the source) fall on every heavy syllable (CVC, CVV(C); CVʔ is light) wherever it stands, obligatorily (ʔílʸápáŋ 'shotgun'); any other nonfinal light syllable may optionally be stressed (kábúčúwa ~ kábučúwa 'rope'); stem-initial syllables and lexically stressed suffixes are also stressed (see morphology note). No alternating rhythm is described; the initial outranks the rest only per the tentative section 4.1 (intensity decreases through the word).

60.prule: Key 1961:149: strong stress on the antepenultimate syllable of utterances of three or more syllables and on the initial syllable of shorter ones; Key distinguishes only weak and strong stress and does not rank the antepenultimate stress above the other strong stresses of the tri-syllable count.
60.srule: Ternary rhythm: besides the antepenultimate strong stress, strong stress falls on every third syllable preceding it, counted leftward within the utterance/stress group and restarting from any morpheme that carries its own strong stress; Key distinguishes only weak vs strong stress and does not rank the iterated strong stresses as primary vs secondary (isolated words show the pattern: ma’rahaha’eiki 'their blankets', ‘Badata’oai 'my younger brother').

vlen.q: Cayuvava (Key 1961) has no contrast of syllable weight. Stress falls on the antepenultimate syllable and on every third syllable preceding it. However, disyllabic words are stressed on the penult. Each stress is reported to be equally strong.

evidence_works.detail: Cayuvava is the paradigm strictly ternary system: stress on every third syllable counted from the right edge, up to two syllables left unfooted at the left edge, the rightmost stress primary (after Levin 1988). The forms are Key 1961's, relayed; the paper adds no new Cayuvava material.

evidence_works.detail: The paper restates Cayuvava as antepenultimate primary stress with secondary stresses every third syllable to its left, the pattern the catalog codes as 10 100 0100 00100 100100 0100100 00100100. It ranks the antepenultimate stress as primary, whereas the catalog notes that Key himself does not rank the iterated strong stresses.

tn.quote: Dialects of Chamalal have been analyzed as possessing various tonal properties, with some contradictory descriptions. Kibrik et al. (1978: 44) analyze Low Gakwari Chamalal as contrasting four tones (H, L, R, F) on the stressed syllable only, while Kibrik & Kodzasov (1990: 325) describe it as specifying each syllable for one of the four tones, and list a number of tone-based minimal pairs … For Gigatli Chamalal, Kibrik & Kodzasov (1990: 324) postulate both a system of four tones, as in Low Gakwari Chamalal, and word stress.
tn.cite: Borise, Lena. 2021. Tone and intonation in the languages of the Caucasus. In M. Polinsky (ed.), The Oxford Handbook of Languages of the Caucasus. Oxford: OUP (preprint lingbuzz/004204, 30 pp.)
tn.locator: sec. 2.4 'Conflicting descriptions and accounts', preprint p. 7; tone labels defined sec. 2.2, p. 4
tn.note: Accounts conflict: four tones (high, low, rising, falling) on every syllable with separate word stress (Kibrik & Kodzasov 1990), on the stressed syllable only (1978), two tones, or stress alone.

61.cfw: Bokarev 1949, Magomedbekova 1967 and Magomedova 1981/1999/2004 all describe Chamalal stress as mobile and word-distinguishing, with minimal pairs such as χòχa 'bean-pod' vs χoχà 'straw', and Borise 2021 follows them, but Kibrik and Kodzasov 1990 reanalyse the Gakvari and Gigatli dialects as four-tone systems with word stress only in Gigatli, and StressTyp2 codes the language as fixed initial, so the lexical reading is well supported but not uncontested.

62.dq: Chamorro is a language with stress. Each word has one syllable that bears primary stress (i.e. is louder or more prominent than the other syllables in the word). This syllable is generally the penultimate (next-to-last) syllable of the word. Primary stress is determined differently for roots (unaffixed words) than for affixed words. A substantial number of roots, most of them borrowed from Spanis…
62.dloc: Chung 2020, Chamorro Grammar (open-access, eScholarship), §29.4.1 Stress p.660
62.heavy: none: the source states no weight criterion for stress placement; vowel length is derived (open penults lengthen under primary stress), not a conditioner; examples show penult stress on light open penults (/iˈlotis/, /kaˈdidak/) and lexically listed antepenult roots of the same shape (/ˈkunanaf/)
62.prule: Roots: primary stress on the penultimate syllable; a lexically listed set of roots (mostly Spanish loans) has final stress and another listed set has antepenultimate stress. Affixed words: suffix -> penult of the suffixed word; inherently stressed prefix -> the prefix; other affixes leave root stress in place; the last-added affix decides.
62.srule: Rhythmic secondary stress on any syllable not adjacent to another stressed syllable, i.e. on alternate syllables counted from the primary (/ˌsiminˈteddzu/ 'cemetery', /ˌbilimˈbinis/ 'star apple', /eŋˌkisiˈfwesi/ 'no matter', /ˈɒʔpaˌkaʔ/ 'white'). In affixed words, additionally, the syllable that bore primary stress in the unaffixed word keeps a secondary stress unless it immediately precedes the new primary (/ˌdeddiˈgo-kku/ 'my heel', /ˌpatgun-ˈmidzu/ vs. /patˈgon-hu/); it may directly follow the primary after a stressed prefix or the progressive reduplicant (/ˈkeʔ-ˌtuŋuʔ/, /ˈdɒˌdaŋkulu/).

morph.rootq: §29.4.1 pp.660-663: 'Primary stress is determined differently for roots (unaffixed words) than for affixed words. ... In affixed words, primary stress is determined by whether the affix is a suffix, an inherently stressed prefix, or some other morpheme. (i) When the affix is a suffix, primary stress falls on the penultimate syllable of the suffixed word. ... (ii) When the affix is a stressed prefix, primary stress falls on the prefix ... (iii) Other affixes do not affect the stress pattern: primary stress falls on the same syllable as in the unaffixed word [e.g. /man-atɾaˈsɒw/, /man-ma-kaˈdidak/]. evidence_works.detail: The paper is about where Chamorro weak pronouns go (after the first phonological phrase) and uses word stress only as a diagnostic: every prosodic word carries one primary stress computed from the right edge, and progressive reduplication copies the primary-stressed CV, which shows where that stress falls. tn.quote: There are ten tonemes in Chatino. ... The tone system of Chatino combines register and contour tones. There are four register tones, which are pronounced with a relatively level pitch, and are indicated by superscript 1 (high), 2 (mid), 3 (low-mid), and 4 (low). ... In addition to the four register tones, there are two rising contour tones, indicated by superscript 21 and 32, and three falling contours, 12, 23, and 34. Finally, certain verbs in the Continuative aspect and a few mono-morphemic lexical items realize a more sharply falling contour tone, which I indicate by superscript 24.
tn.cite: Rasch, Jeffrey Walter. 2002. The basic morpho-syntax of Yaitepec Chatino. PhD dissertation, Rice University.
tn.note: Ten tonemes (4 level, 5 contours + sharp fall 24 mostly on Continuative verbs); one tone per phonological word, on its final full vowel. Author calls the analysis incomplete; p. 7 says nine tones. Checked against the source (tone consistency check, 2026-09-23): domain stem or root -> word melody (Introduction 'Overview of the chapters', pp. xv-xvi; Ch. 1 sec. 3.1.2, p. 9 and …).

corr.words: Each phonological word carries a single tone, either a level register tone or a rising or falling contour tone. Besides being lexically contrastive, tones are conditioned by aspectual and person-marking morphology. Some allomorphs are realized only as tone. ... in a single phonological word, only one vowel (the final one) is unreduced. ... Reduced vowels are not specified for tone.
corr.loc: Introduction 'Overview of the chapters', pp. xv-xvi; Ch. 1 sec. 3.1.2, p. 9 and p. 10

morph.rootq: §1.4.3 p.39: 'Stress is non-contrastive and occurs on the first of a sequence of combined syllables - that is, word initially.' Also §5.4.1.3 p.169: 'certain rules apply only to stressed syllables, which are the first of a string of combined elements.' The statement is framed on the word/string of combined syllables, not the root; the only mention of affixes is the imperative exception, §3.2.3.2 p.101: 'The last syllable of an Imperative utterance is stressed, even if it is an affix and not a free particle.' (Since 'there is in fact no prefixing in the language at all' (p.41), word-initial coincides with root-initial, but the grammar does not say so.)
morph.elicq: The stress statement (§1.4.3 p.39, 'Stress is non-contrastive and occurs on the first of a sequence of combined syllables - that is, word initially') gives no evidence basis. General data statement §1.1.10 p.8: 'The data on which this thesis is based comes almost entirely from Maiserang village in the Makwanpur district ... collected over a period of eight years (1968-1976)'; suprasegmentals are referred to an earlier paper ('A description of suprasegmentals, Caughley (1970b)', p.7). The only stress-marked datum is a sentence example (ex. 44 p.51, 'where heavy stress is indicated by (") before the syllable and lighter stress by (')').
morph.stmt: Exclusively suffixing and highly agglutinative: 'Causative, Negative, Interrogative and Reciprocal markers... all of these occur as verbal suffixes - there is in fact no prefixing in the language at all' (§1.5.1.1 p.41); 'the case forms are suffixed to the NP' (p.41); 'Chepang, like many other OV languages (Lehmann, 1973) is highly agglutinative' (§1.5.1.2 p.41); verb template Root (InF)(Conj)(Der)(Aux){Tense Pron/Pron Neg}(Int) (§1.5.2 p.46).

tn.quote: The phonological analysis summarised in the previous section views Chepang as a non-tonal language ... Pitch is contrastive in Chepang only in restricted environments for certain syllable types. The glottal stop, for which the contrastive falling pitch may be a realisation, evidently derives historically from former affixes. If the falling pitch occurred in all environments then the language would be tonal. Chepang today therefore is in an intermediate stage, between an earlier non-tonal form of the language, with affixes, and a possible later development to a fully tonal language.
tn.cite: Caughley, Ross Charles. 1982. The Syntax and Morphology of the Verb in Chepang. Pacific Linguistics, Series B - No. 84. Canberra: Department of Linguistics, Research School of Pacific Studies, The Australian National University.
tn.note: Analysed as non-tonal: a contrastive falling pitch occurs only in restricted environments, as the usual realisation of syllable-final glottal stop; an intermediate stage toward tone. tn.quote: Tones do not play the part in the phonemic system that may be expected of a Sino - Tibetan language . In fact, only in the southern dialect two phonemic tones can be distinguished, and even these are to a great extent grammatical- ly or phonologically predictable . morph.stmt: 'Chitimacha is a strongly synthetic, strongly head-marking language that is consistently suffixing rather than prefixing (Swadesh 1946a:314)' (Hieber 2019:319); all verbal inflection (patient, aspect, agent/subject, mood, switch-reference) and derivation (causative -pa, benefactive -aʔ, pluractional -ma, nominalisers) is suffixal, nominal case/topic marking is enclitic, and the only pre-root grammatical material is the closed set of monosyllabic 'context words' (Swadesh 1934:347): the nine preverbs (hi, kap, ni, ʔap, ʔapš, kas...) before the verb and the demonstrative proclitic we 'that, the' before the noun, both written as separate words by Hieber.

70.dq: First, all lexical words have lexical prominence or primary stress ('obligatoriness parameter') with one syllable bearing the highest degree of prominence – 'culminativity parameter' (Hyman 2006). ... Stress assignment in the nominal domain varies across the alienable vs. inalienable paradigm. In alienable nouns, primary stress is final. ... Prefixes define the leftmost edge of the Prosodic Word;…
70.heavy: Heavy = syllable with a glottalized (creaky/rearticulated) vowel, i.e. vowel + tautosyllabic glottal stop, analysed as bimoraic ('the moraic weight of the feature [constricted glottis]'; Cuadernos 2019: 'las vocales glotalizadas tienen peso... las consonantes en posición de coda no son moraicas'). Plain coda consonants are NOT moraic, but a word-initial CVC syllable (incl. CVʔ, CV̰) forms a monosyllabic foot and receives secondary stress (MinFt=CVC), whereas an initial CV does not — syllable shape, not weight, per the author. Vowel length is not contrastive.
70.dflt: final syllable (right-edge iamb): siˈse 'cane', kʼak.xó 'armadillo', t͡ʃʼa.tʼá 'tortuga'; in prefixed inalienables footing from the prefix edge can yield penult (ji-ˈka-saʃ)
70.prule: Iambic feet, quantity-sensitive; primary stress on the rightmost foot. In unprefixed (alienable) nouns iambs are built from the right edge of the Morphological Root / Stem, so primary stress is final (siˈse, sisI-ˈʧat, kʼak.xó) unless a preceding heavy (glottalized-vowel) syllable takes it (xiˈβeʔk͡lə 'moon', penult). Derivational suffixes move stress rightward to the last syllable of the Morphological Base. In inalienable (obligatorily prefixed) nouns the possessive prefix defines the left edge of the Prosodic Word and footing proceeds from that edge (ji-ˈka-saʃ, penult). Fabre independently: 'El acento principal de la palabra nivacle recae generalmente en la última sílaba. No es distintivo', with exceptions (suffix -c’oya attracts stress; glottalized /ɒ̰/ and /a/ before /m/ tend to attract it; some roots/affixed forms penult-stressed, 'quedan muchas interrogantes').
70.srule: At most one secondary stress, at the left edge: in polysyllabic words a word-initial closed syllable (CVC, CVʔ, CV̰C) forms a monosyllabic minimal foot with secondary stress ((ʔɑ̀k)(xe.k͡lɑ́) 'woman', (pùʔ)(xa.ná) 'three', (fà̰j)(ku-kát)); an initial open CV syllable gets none (si(βo.k͡lók) 'spider', ni(βa.k͡lé) 'man'); in possessive-prefixed/long words a left-edge-aligned iamb may carry it instead ([βa.tà.si.nɑ́] 'someone's word'). Primary on the rightmost foot; stressed syllables never adjacent (*Clash); medial syllables unparsed -- no iterative alternating secondaries. Initial-CVC secondary is optional (Gutiérrez 2015: 154 fn. 51).
70.quote: First, all lexical words have lexical prominence or primary stress (‘obligatoriness parameter’) with one syllable bearing the highest degree of prominence – ‘culminativity parameter’ (Hyman 2006). Second, stressed vowels are longer than unstressed vowels. As previously mentioned, glottalized vowels always occur under stress and are double the duration of modal vowels, hence my analysis of them as bimoraic. In terms of metrical structure, I propose that (i) the Nivaĉle foot type is iambic, and (ii) the Nivaĉle language has a quantity-sensitive stress system, where the moraic weight of the feat…
70.loc: JIPA 49(3), p. 413, section 'Stress' (and end of the glottalized-vowel section on the same page)
70.idn: Nivaĉle, shichaam lhavos variety ('the lowlanders/Downriver'); author also worked with yita’ lhavos speakers (a named variety of the language); data: Two shichaam lhavos speakers (FR, 72, and TS, 50) recorded in Uj’e Lhavos, a Nivaĉle community 1 km from Filadelfia, Boquerón Department, Paraguay; recording dates not…
70.exq_: Fabre 2016:78-80 (corroborating, named in cite): 'No obstante, existen algunas excepciones a esta regla. Una de ellas implica el sufijo -c’oya (5.4.3.), que atrae el acento principal de la palabra en su primera sílaba. ... /ɒ̰/ ... tiende a atraer el acento. ... quedan muchas interrogantes.'

none — no quantity-insensitive pattern per length exists to reclassify to. The rule as described (Wash 2001:33, following Harrington): final stress iff both of the final two syllables have codas, OR the word-final consonant is glottalized, OR the final-syllable onset is aspirated (incl. h); otherwise penultimate. 71.dq: Harrington (33.0235) first noted that there are two main patterns of predictable word stress in Barbareño: stress that occurs on the penultimate syllable, and stress that occurs on the final syllable.
71.dloc: Wash 2001:33 §2.1.4, carried from note on the cited source; Applegate 2017:25 §1.3 opened, "The accent on Shmuwich words generally goes on the second syllable from the end, but the situation is a bit more complex."
71.heavy: A syllable that 'has a coda' (closed syllable); Wash speaks of 'the weight of the final two syllables'. Final stress requires BOTH the penult and the final to be closed; a single closed syllable (ʔé.neq, yín.ċi) does not attract stress. Independently of weight, final stress is also triggered by glottalization of the word-final consonant and by aspiration (incl. h) on the final-syllable onset (laryngeal/onset conditions, not rime weight). No vowel-length criterion is mentioned.
71.prule: Two 'main patterns' (Wash 2001:33, after Harrington): penultimate stress 'generally' when at least one of the last two syllables is open; final stress when both of the last two syllables are closed, or when the word-final consonant is glottalized, or when the final-syllable onset is aspirated/h. Applegate 2017:25-26 states the same default penult and the h/aspirate-onset final rule as predictable, but treats all other final-accent words as an 'occasional', 'not predictable', lexically written class (most of his marked examples do satisfy Wash's both-closed or final-glottalization conditions), and his suffixed paradigms (kitaqínwaš, šlekʼenpiyítwaš, kalaqwaywaš, šuquštaywaš) carry penult accent despite both final syllables being closed.
71.srule: Not mentioned in Wash 2001, sec. 2.1.4 'Stress' (p. 33, whole section read), nor in Applegate 2017, sec. 1.3 'The Accent' (pp. 25-26): both describe only the placement of the (single marked) word stress — penult vs. final — and every cited word, up to five syllables (ʔax.ta.wa.yán.pi; šlekʼenpiyítwaš), carries one stress mark; neither states a one-stress-per-word rule or any rhythmic/secondary stress.

morph.stmt: Applegate 2017 §2.2 p.48: "Shmuwich relies heavily on prefixes to add to the meaning of roots, especially with verbs. Verbs can include multiple prefixes in front of a root... Shmuwich has many prefixes, but far fewer suffixes." The verb template (§7.9 p.159) is PERSON-NUMBER-NEG-FUT-[middle/inner prefixes]-ROOT-OBJECT-PAST; nouns take possessive person-number prefixes and the article l- before the root, with plural mostly by prefixed CVC reduplication.

st.weight_quote: Penultimate stress occurs generally when at least one of the final two syllables lacks a coda. ... Final stress occurs when both of the final two syllables have a coda. ... Final stress also occurs when the word-final consonant has glottalization, regardless of the weight of the final two syllables, ... or when the onset of the final syllable has aspiration.

tn.quote: 3. Intonation At least three pitch contours may be recognized: a) a rising curve, marked, appearing (infrequently) on words expressing assent or agreement; b) a curve, rising and then falling, marked, on words expressing surprise, interrogation, or astonishment; c) a falling curve, marked hitherto identified on the final syllables of nouns with initial (distributive) reduplication. … Nouns may show initial reduplication accompanied by glottalization and falling tone on the final syllable; this formation, though it has been called a plural, appears rather to have distributive meaning.

tn.quote: Jacquesson (2005) states that there is a two-way tonal contrast in Deori - high and low. ... Results show that tonal distinctions are maintained in the homophonous words. However, unlike other Tibeto-Burman languages, (Bodo, Dimasa, and Tiwa) the tonal contours in Deori are not static across all the tonally distinctive lexical items and tone is spread across the word in which lexical distinctions are preserved. The domain of tone bearing unit in Deori is the phonological word rather than the syllable ... there are very few homophonous words with tonal contrasts.
tn.cite: Acharyya, Prarthana. 2020 (submitted 2019). Phonology of Deori: an 'endangered' language. PhD thesis, IIT Guwahati (TH-2450_136141007), 240 pp.; ch. 4 Production and Perception of Tones in Deori
tn.note: High vs low tone on a small set of homophone pairs, carried by the whole word and cued by f0 only; older speakers keep it, younger speakers reverse or merge it. Coexists with predictable iambic stress

73.dq: In KK, word stress has delimitative functions. In general, stress is fixed and occurs on the penultimate syllable of a word. Therefore, stress constitutes the basic criterion to identify word boundaries in KK.
73.dloc: §3.3.1 p. 119; see also §3.3.2 p. 120: "In polysyllabic words that contain one morpheme, stress follows the pattern described above: it always goes on the penultimate syllable".
73.prule: Primary stress falls on the penultimate syllable of the word (monomorphemic words always); a closed set of inherently stressed suffixes and enclitics (Table 3.3: -n, -tú, -pán, =já, =új, =ikwá, =tsurj-áj, =á, =nán, particle áj) takes final stress when it closes the word.
73.srule: In polymorphemic words of more than four syllables a secondary stress can fall two syllables before the penultimate primary (ja.wa.ra.`pa.na, ka.ri.ka.ri.`ta.ka); stated as 'it is possible to find', so not marked in the rule string.

Stress in monomorphemic words. In polysyllabic words that contain one morpheme, stress follows the pattern described above: it always goes on the penultimate syllable, as illustrated in (53). (53) `a.mi ‗grandfather‘ `tse.nu ‗hear‘ ja.`ka.ri ‗alligator‘ ʧi.`kwa.ra ‗buttock‘ ta.ma.…

73.exq_: The stress pattern changes in a few cases, under specific morphophonological conditions. ... in KK some morphemes have stress as part of their forms. ... The stressed morpheme has to close the word; that is, it needs to occur at the end of the word in order for stress to appear in the last syllable.

74.dloc: Borman 1962, Cofan phonemes, section 7.1, p. 57 (the archived SIL scan)
74.heavy: The source never uses 'heavy/light' or vowel length. The conditioning is glottal closure of the penultimate STEM syllable: penult open (no glottal closure) -> penultimate stress (class one); penult closed by glottal stop -> antepenultimate stress (class two). Polarity is the reverse of the usual weight effect (the glottal-closed syllable repels stress rather than attracting it). Borman's syllable types are CV, CVʔ, CV1V2, CV1V2ʔ (p.57), so glottal stop is the only coda; nothing is said about CV1V2 (diphthongal) penults behaving differently from CV.

evidence_works.work: Repetti-Ludlow & Chelsea Sanker 2019, A'ingae (Cofán) (Journal of the International Phonetic Association 50(3): 431-444. doi:10.1017/S0025100319000082)
evidence_works.independence: not assessed (journal search; a single reading)
evidence_works.detail: The paper measures three speakers and finds stress cued mainly by longer vowels and also by a higher f0 peak, with no amplitude effect, and places stress usually on the penultimate or antepenultimate syllable of the root, never word-finally except in monosyllables. It shows stress is partly lexical (ˈnepije 'to disappear' vs neˈpije 'to arrive') and moved by affixes and clitics, which agrees with the catalog's penultimate default and glottal-conditioned antepenult while adding the phonetic correlates and disputing Fischer & Hengeveld's stem-final verb stress.

evidence_works.detail: Two native speakers' judgments (no acoustic measurement) show that A'ingae verbs get default penultimate stress, that some roots carry lexical initial stress, that a glottal stop in the root or an inner suffix pulls stress onto the syllable holding the second mora to its left, and that dominant suffixes wipe out stress, which is then reassigned within the inner domain (never word-final) or to the penult; secondary stress alternates outward from the primary. 75.srule: Secondary stresses exist (Blake 1999: 26 fn. 12, 'generally not transcribed' there). Placement per later work: a left-aligned trochaic, binary alternating pattern counted from the initial primary in words of three or more syllables — σ́σσ̀, σ́σσ̀σ (Blake 2000: 173 ex. 114; McCarthy & Schnoor 2023: 334 and Watanabe 2026: 99 after Watanabe 2003: 21-29) — with morphologically conditioned departures: bisyllabic lexical suffixes and =uɬ attract stress, =inas avoids a clash, stative -it takes an adjacent secondary stress/[HH] pitch, indirective -ʔəm attracts secondary stress (Blake 2000: 173-176; Menon 2023: 341). Blake 2000: 177-178 cautions that secondary-stress generalizations 'are not well understood'.

morph.stmt: Heavily prefixing verb with a substantial suffix system: 'the tightly-knit inner verbal complex consists minimally of a subject prefix and a stem. This inner complex includes thirteen position classes of prefixes and seven position classes of suffixes. A given verb word may have nine or ten prefixes and four or five suffixes' (p.369), preceded by proclitic complexes (subject, negation, locative base); person (subject, object, possessor, reflexive), completive/perfective aspect, narrative/assertive mode and a six-slot locative system are prefixal, while tense, remaining aspect, causative, applicative, passive, participles, noun plural, absolutive and derivation are suffixal.

tn.quote: The suprasegmentals of Cora include both stress and tone which, although in many cases correlate with one another, fail to do so often enough that it is necessary to separate them analytically. Within a given phrase there are three perceptual degrees of stress: primary, secondary, and unstressed. There are two levels of tone that function syntactically - high and low. In addition, there are four sequences of tones on long syllabic nucleii: high-high; high-low; low-high and low-low. ... 2.4. Tone There are two levels of tone - high and low - that function morphophonemically in Cora.
tn.cite: Casad, Eugene H. n.d. [ca. 1980]. Cora Phonology. Unpublished ms., 74 pp. Bartholomew Collection of Unpublished Materials, SIL International - Mexico Branch (SIL Language & Culture Archives 53630).
tn.locator: ms p. 2 (end of the phoneme/orthography introduction) and sec. 2.4 'Tone', ms p. 21
tn.note: Two level tones, high and low; long nuclei carry HH, HL, LH or LL (high-falling = HL). Tone shown to be independent of stress. Preuss 1912 marks only a dynamic (stress) accent, no tone.

76.cfw: Preuss 1912 says the accent falls "very frequently" on the antepenult but marks exceptions, double-peaked words and fluctuation, Casad 1984 gives no positional rule at all, and Kim and Valdovinos 2014 treat Mariteco Cora stress as lexical and find roughly half of monomorphemic disyllables final-stressed, so the fixed antepenultimate coding that comes from Gordon 2002 is contested on the type of system.

77.dq: Every phonological word, sentence-level phrase, and sentence in Coreguaje has a tendency to fade away; that is, as a unit progresses, the syllables tend to become lower in pitch, shorter in length, and diminished in volume. The first syllable of a stem of a word is usually stressed. Stress is characterized by perceived loudness and length. High pitches tend to be higher toward the beginning of th…

77.prule: Primary stress falls on the first syllable of the stem ('The first syllable of a stem of a word is usually stressed'); in all of Gralow's examples the stem is word-initial (the affixes shown are suffixes), so the stressed syllable is the word-initial one.
77.srule: No rhythmic secondary stress is stated. Besides the stem-initial stress, the three disyllabic suffixes with inherent high tone (-kʰáí benefactive, -háí accompanying movement, -kóso probability) 'seem to have stress on the first syllable as do stems' (Gralow 1985:8); the position is morphological, so it is not marked in the rule string.
77.quote: In the process of the analysis it finally became evident that stress was basically predictable, though tone was not. [...] Every phonological word, sentence-level phrase, and sentence in Coreguaje has a tendency to fade away; that is, as a unit progresses, the syllables tend to become lower in pitch, shorter in length, and diminished in volume. The first syllable of a stem of a word is usually stressed. Stress is characterized by perceived loudness and length. High pitches tend to be higher toward the beginning of the word, phrase, or sentence than they are toward the end.

77.exq_: Two-syllable suffixes which have inherent high tone tend to act differently from suffixes without inherent high tone. They also seem to have stress on the first syllable as do stems. ... These suffixes are: -kʰáí benefactive, -háí accompanying movement, -kóso probability
77.tone: Two contrastive tone levels, high and low; disyllabic stems contrast in all four sequences (ñámá 'deer', náso 'monkeys', rutʰá 'flies', wekʰɨ 'tapirs'). Gralow: 'stress was basically predictable, though tone was not'; contrastive intonation contours 'affect and even override word tone patterns', and phrase stress neutralizes the tone contrasts on CVCV nouns in isolation.

The stress rule itself is cited to 'PHC 5.3.2 and 6.2.7; PSR 5.3 and 5.5' and to the parallel with Welsh and Breton. tn.quote: There is very little textual evidence as to how Cornish was stressed. Evidence from place-names suggests that the pattern was the same as in Breton (though not the Gwenedeg dialect thereof). We may surmise that, in common with Breton and Welsh, the normal stress in polysyllables was originally on the ultimate syllable, and that it changed, perhaps c. 1050, to the penultimate. Unpublished work by Keith Bailey on stress in Middle Cornish verse suggests that, as in Welsh, the stress-accent was usually on the penultimate syllable, but the pitch-accent remained on the ultimate.
tn.cite: George, Ken. 2009. 'Cornish'. In Ball & Müller (eds.), The Celtic Languages, 2nd ed. London/New York: Routledge, ch. 11, pp. 488-535

contra.head: StressTyp2 codes a fixed pattern that later instrumental studies dispute
contra.detail: StressTyp2 codes antepenultimate primary stress with secondary pattern i2@m; the descriptions it cites do state antepenultimate word stress (Okimasis & Ratt 1999 [2018 ed., pp. 6-7]: primary stress on the third syllable from the right, a secondary on the fifth from the right in five-syllable words, final stress in disyllables; Wolfart 1996: 431: secondary stress on alternate syllables in either direction from the antepenult). The instrumental studies of Mühlbauer 2006, Athanasopoulou et al. 2025 and Schmirler & Arnhold 2025 instead find a penultimate falling pitch (word-level pitch accent) or no word stress. The sources conflict, so the language is not listed under fixed stress.

morph.stmt: Plains Cree is polysynthetic and head-marking with a fixed verb template 'Person + Tense - Preverb - Verb Stem + Suffix' (Okimasis 2018 p.28-29): a single person prefix slot (ni-/ki-/o-, also marking possessors on nouns) and a string of preverbs (tense kī-/ka-/wī-, conjunct ē-/kā-, modal/aspectual nōhtē-, pē- etc.) precede the stem, while all other inflection and derivation is suffixal — direction/theme signs, person-number-obviation endings, imperative/conditional mode, noun plural -ak/-a, obviative -a, locative -ihk, diminutive -is(is), nominaliser -win, causative -h, benefactive -amaw, reflexive -iso, reciprocal -ito, unspecified-actor -ikawi…

evidence_works.detail: Pitch, duration and intensity each show regular patterns (rising f0 on the antepenult and the final syllable, falling f0 on the penult, longer and quieter final syllables) but never converge on one syllable, so the authors reject antepenultimate, penultimate and ultimate stress and analyse Plains Cree as a phrase language with no word stress and no lexical tone or pitch accent: the pitch contours are phrase-edge tones (H at the start, LHLH at the end of the phonological phrase, with intonation-phrase final lowering).

tn.quote: Based on the acoustic evidence, we suggest that Plains Cree is a pitch-accent system, with a predictable penultimate HL word-level pitch-accent. Tonal patterns in other syllables are the result of prosodic boundaries, phonetic interpolation, or tonal spreading. ... Notably, only the penult is tonally specified, and it is always HL. ... 80.dq: A measure cannot contain less than a word, but more than one word may be contained in a measure
80.prule: Primary (strong) stress on the initial syllable of the phonological word at every length (Kucera 1961:54 strong-stress onset = phonemic-measure boundary; p.58 phonological word = segment that can alone constitute a measure or pre-measure segment). Secondary (medial) stress: OPTIONAL, careful pronunciation only, freely replaced by weak stress in casual speech without phonemic distinction; when present it falls non-contrastively on either the 2nd or the 3rd syllable after the strong-stressed syllable (sigma3 or sigma4), provided no further strong stress intervenes; the source licenses no medial stress outside this window and states no iteration and no binary alternation ("medial stress" occurs only on pp.52-54 of the whole volume; zero volume hits for alternation/rhythm wording). Licensed grids: n=3: 100~101; n=4: 1000~1010~1001; n=5: 10000~10100~10010; n=6+: 10...0 with at most one secondary on sigma3 or sigma4. StressTyp2's coding 10101/1010101 is unlicensed at n>=5 on two independent counts (iterated medial stress; stress outside the sigma+2/sigma+3 window). The grid records the strong (primary) stress only (10 100 1000 10000...); the optional medial stress is described under Secondary stress and is not part of the fixed pattern.
80.srule: Secondary ('medial') stress is optional and non-contrastive: in careful pronunciation it may occur on either the second or the third syllable after the strong-stressed syllable (provided no other strong stress comes first), and on the first syllable of a pre-measure segment; in more casual pronunciation it may be replaced by weak stress (Kučera 1961:54 §2.244). It is not part of the fixed pattern; the source states no alternating rhythm.
80.quote: If the place of onset of strong stress (i.e. of loud and overloud stresses) is established, the occurrence of medial and weak stresses becomes predictable. Medial stress may occur, in careful pronunciation, on either the second or third syllable (non-contrastively) after the syllable with strong stress, provided that another strong stress does not occur first
80.loc: p. 54, §2.244 'Phonemic status of stresses. Phonemic measures'

morph.stmt: Predominantly suffixing: all inflection (seven cases x two numbers on nouns/adjectives, person/number, past -l, gender/number, imperative, participles) is by endings after the stem, and 'any suffix is additionally an identifier of what part of speech the item belongs to', while prefixes are limited to negation ne-, the score of aspectual/lexical verbal prefixes (do-, na-, po-, za-...) and nominal/adjectival prefixes — in the grammar's words (§2.2, p.42): 'Derivational morphology in Czech is accomplished by means of prefixation and suffixation of roots... prefixes largely serve to augment or supplement the meaning of the lexical item, and any suffix is additionally an identifier of what…

The rule is stated on the word, but the discussion ties the stressed penult to the root and the unstressed final to the suffix: p.19 'lexical tones, both H and L, associate to the stressed penult and final syllables get whatever is the contextually appropriate derived tone, i.e. the polarity tone. This agrees in spirit with Newman's (1995) suggestion that the…
morph.elicq: Anttila & Bodomo 1996 fn.1: 'The dialect described in this paper is the Central dialect spoken in and around Jirapa, northwestern Ghana. The native speaker judgments are those of the second author.' The evidence for penultimate stress is phonological-distributional, not phonetic: §2.5 'The first hint about stress in Dagaare comes from segmental asymmetries. According to Kennedy (1966, 3-4), the simple word consists of a primary syllable followed by an optional secondary syllable ... Another diagnostic for stress is tone. tn.quote: Dagaare (Gur, Niger-Congo) is a two-tone language spoken in northwestern Ghana and adjoining areas of Burkina Faso. Minimal pairs like bá 'to move fast' vs. bà 'to put up a pole' and báá 'a dog' vs. bàà 'to grow up' are prima facie evidence for a lexical contrast between H and L tones. However, in the nominal system, tonal contrasts are most of the time restricted to the penultimate syllable, the remaining tones being predictable. ... Following Kennedy (1966), we posit the syllable as the TBU. ... Dagaare has both downstep and downdrift (Kennedy 1966).

tn.note: Two level tones H and L; syllable is the TBU; root tones lexical, suffix tones polar or spread; downstep analysed as floating L (class D nouns HLH); separate penultimate stress attracts lexical tones.

82.dq: (d) Dakota (Siouan, Great Plains; Chambers 1978; Shaw 1985a, 1985b). Stress falls on the second syllable of a word, and on monosyllables. This suggests that a single even iamb is assigned at the left edge of a word.
82.dloc: Hayes 1995:267, §6.3.11(d) 'Even Iambs?'; fn. 19 same page: 'Since there is no phonemic vowel length in Dakota'; cf. 82.srule: Riggs 1893:5 §4.3(a): 'In polysyllabic words there is usually a secondary accent, which falls on the second syllable after the primary one' (hewóskantúya, íćiyópeya; one secondary described, iteration not stated); §4.3(b): in noun+noun / noun+verb compounds each member keeps its own accent. The later metrical literature treats Dakota stress as one noniterative foot with a single stress per word and no rhythmic secondary (Kennedy 1994:47-48 after Shaw 1985: owį́čhayaktepiktešni; Hayes 1995:267 'a single even iamb'; Rhyasen Erdman 1997:iii 'do not generate secondary stress'), a second stress only in syntactic compounds (Kennedy 1994:50).

83.quote: 1.4 Stress. The following rules for Stress have been found: i. In words of two syllables, stress falls on the first: /jɛlɛg/, 'slowly'; ... /'mimal/, 'firewood'. ... ii. In words of three syllables, stress is normally on the first ... iii. In three syllable words a final glottalised consonant tends to attract the stress: /bigɔ'niŋˀ/, 'who?'. iv. In words of more than three syllables, a secondary stress may occur in the third syllable ..., thus: /"mɔna'ŋa:gɨn/, 'for the white man'. v. Final stress occurs on the future suffix -jan, as in /ŋaˀbɔni'jan/, 'I shall go'

84.srule: In most words of three or more syllables (not contour-final) the initial syllable has increased loudness and a secondary upward pitch glide, the medial syllables being weaker than both the first and the final (primary-stressed) syllable; disyllables have no initial prominence. In addition, an unpredictable, contrastive 'independent secondary stress' (added length and loudness) falls on a non-final syllable of certain words that include a monosyllabic clitic (fn. 45: possibly a shifted primary stress; no valid predictability statement). Clitics bear neither primary nor secondary stress.

There is a prevalence of final stress when the final syllable is closed. If the final syllable is open, and the vowel short, the stress is non-fi…
85.dloc: the StressTyp2 entry "Danish (ST1)" (Rischel 1982), words vioˈliː̀n, peˈtroː̀leum, ˈfoto, komˈplot
85.heavy: Ranked: (1) a syllable with a long vowel takes the stress; (2) otherwise a closed syllable takes precedence over an open syllable; open final syllable with short vowel repels stress; schwa syllables (-er, -e) never stressed; only full-vowel syllables are candidates. Rischel adds that underlying long consonants can make a syllable count as 'underlyingly heavy' (p. 200).
85.dflt: With no long vowel and an open short-vowel final: non-final (penult: fóto, gálla); Rischel 1970's rule set as summarized p. 200 has a last default rule assigning final stress if nothing else applies.
85.prule: In simplex words/polysyllabic morphemes: stress the syllable with a long vowel; if none, closed beats open, with a general prevalence of final stress when the last syllable is closed (parýk, bandít, komplót, parasól); if the final syllable is open with a short vowel, stress is non-final (fóto, gálla); Rischel 1970's ordered disjunctive rules (long V > long C > syllable boundaries/clusters) end with a default rule assigning final stress. Wordforms with more than one long vowel are accented like compounds.
85.srule: Only in compounds and quasi-compounds. A non-compound wordform has one full stress and all other syllables weak (= zero) stress, ungraded ('no need for a grading of stresses beyond the distinction between full stress and weak stress'; Intra-Word UA keeps only the last inherent morpheme stress: violinistínde; no rhythmic perturbations found). Graded secondary stresses occur in compounds (leftmost strong, later members reduced by rank: [ˈhunəˌˌhalsˌbʌnˀ] hundehalsband) and quasi-compounds (-dom/-hed/-skab derivatives; wordforms with two long vowels).

morph.rootq: Rischel 1982 p. 196 (section 'B. Morpheme stress'): 'a morpheme cannot be inherently stressed unless it contains at least one full vowel. This takes care of inflectional endings, which contain only consonants and schwa. There are also a couple of derivational suffixes, viz. -(l)ig and -(n)ing, which are unstressed ... As for prefixes, I wish to contend that these are, as a rule, inherently stressed but undergo the process of Intra-Word Unit Accentuation'; p. 196: Low German prefixes '(e.g. be-) ... do not normally occur under stress and which might thus be defined as inherently unstressed'; p. 197: 'Suffixes containing a full vowel syllable are inherently stressed'…
morph.elicq: Rischel 1982 p. 191 (abstract, verified): 'The model is essentially based on impressionistic data and phonological and syntactico-semantic analysis of data representing the author's own usage.' p. 192: 'the types of data referred to here are supposed to represent a neutral, colourless rendering of phrases and utterances'. (Introspective judgments by a native-speaker phonetician on words and phrases; tokens themselves are KorpusDK running text from Müller & Ørsnes; no instrumental measurement.)
morph.stmt: Müller & Ørsnes 2013, Preface p. viii: 'It has little inflection. Finite verbs inflect for tense and passive and nouns inflect for genitive/non-genitive and for definiteness (only personal pronouns have an accusative form). Adjectives inflect for number and gender and also for definiteness in attributive use.' All of this inflection is suffixal (Haugen 1976 §6.4(4): the definite article 'with nouns it is suffixed'; §6.4(10) preterite 'dental suffix'; §6.4(12) mediopassive suffix); the only prefixes are a small set of unstressed derivational ones, mostly Middle Low German loans (an-, be-, for-, er-, und-) plus native u- 'un-' (Haugen §6.6, §12.5.1; Rischel 1982 p. 196–198).…

85.cfw: Rischel 1970 and 1982 set out the weight rule for Danish simplex words (a long vowel takes the stress, otherwise the last closed full-vowel syllable, schwa never stressed), Iosad 2016 independently calls the system quantity-sensitive with stress on the rightmost closed syllable, and Grønnum 1998 and Basbøll 2003 likewise describe stress as free but largely predictable with only a handful of lexical minimal pairs; the sole dissent is Gordon 2002's typological appendix, which lists Danish as fixed initial stress on a survey coding that no first-hand description supports.

morph.rootq: Hardeland 1858:18-19 ('Accent oder Betonung'): 'Jedes Wort hat nur auf einer Sylbe den Accent. Derselbe fällt ... auf die vorletzte Sylbe, die ja auch in der Regel die Hauptsylbe des Stammwortes ist. Wo indess, in durch Suffixe abgeleiteten Wörtern, diese Hauptsylbe zur drittletzten Sylbe wird, bleibt der Accent doch auf der Penultima, geht dann also von der ursprünglich betonten auf die tonlose Sylbe des Stammwortes über [kaju > kajúan]. ... Ausnahmen sind: 1. der Accent bleibt auf der letzten Sylbe der wenigen einsylbigen Wörter, auch wenn dieselben durch Präfixe 2 oder mehrsylbig geworden sind; z. B. hai, gross; kahai, Grösse; mampahai, vergrössern. ... 2. ... alle 2 sylbigen Wörter…
morph.elicq: Hardeland 1858 gives no statement of how stress was observed; the description rests on the author's own command of the language from 1850-56 residence ('Spreche ich auch die Sprache ziemlich geläufig ...', Vorwort p. IV) and is illustrated with isolated citation words ('wie die vielen oben angegebenen Beispiele zeigen', p.18). Mihing & Stokhof 1977 likewise state only 'According to our investigation the place of the stress is on the penultimate syllable ...' (p.55) with fn. 2: 'Teres Mihing (38 years old), a native speaker of the Ngaju Dayak (Pulau Petak Dialect) functions as the informant.' Hardeland does add one connected-speech remark for questions: 'Iä häbän? ist er krank?…
morph.stmt: Strongly prefixing: 'Von den Stammwörtern werden abgeleitete Wörter gebildet durch Präfixe, — durch Suffixe, — durch Prä- und Suffixe, — durch ganze oder auch theilweise Reduplication... Die Ableitung durch Präfixe ist die gewöhnliche; Ableitungen durch Reduplication sind auch ziemlich häufig; die andern Arten der Ableitungen kommen nur selten vor' (Hardeland 1858:22), and 'Suffixe giebt es im Dajackschen nur wenige, und auch die wenigen kommen nur selten vor. Das Haupt-Suffix ist an oder n' (p.64); the only frequent post-root bound elements are the pronominal possessor/agent/object suffixes -ku/-ngku, -m, -e and the genitive linker -n, while voice, verbalisation, causative, reciprocal…
